summary: Analyzes the transition to IPv6 in 3GPP packet networks, which are based on GPRS technology with GSM or UMTS/WCDMA radio networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Mobile phone networks must switch to the new address system. This memo looks at what that move involves.

questions: how do mobile networks transition to ipv6
what is a dual stack ue
why is nat-pt not recommended for 3gpp
subtitle: How mobile phone networks can move to IPv6 while handsets and servers still speak IPv4.

tldr.problem: 3GPP packet networks based on GPRS need to introduce IPv6, while handsets, networks and the nodes they talk to may support only IPv4, only IPv6, or both.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through five GPRS and two IMS transition scenarios and says which existing IETF mechanisms (dual stack, tunneling, protocol translators) fit each. It specifies no new mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: The authors recommend dual stack handsets, IPv6 support in operator networks as soon as possible, and tunneling or specific relays rather than general translators like NAT-PT. They also call for a SIP/SDP solution to be worked on.

facts.label: Most relevant scenarios
facts.value: First two GPRS and both IMS

today: RFC 4215 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a 2005 analysis, and it specifies no new transition mechanisms.

sections.title: Scope and Setting
sections.content:
RFC 4215 analyses the move to IPv6 in 3GPP General Packet Radio Service (GPRS) packet networks, whose radio side is GSM or UMTS/WCDMA. The scenarios fall into two groups: general packet service scenarios (called GPRS scenarios) and IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) scenarios, which involve SIP.

The document shall not specify new transition mechanisms. It uses those from the IETF Ngtrans and v6ops working groups and only notes where new ones are needed. It does not cover radio-interface specifics or 3GPP2.

Key terms: a dual stack UE supports both IPv4 and IPv6 and can activate both kinds of PDP context. An IPv6 UE or IPv4 UE supports only one. A PDP context is a connection between the UE and the GGSN, and there are three PDP types: IPv4, IPv6 and PPP.
sections.eli5: Phones, towers and websites do not all speak the same address language yet. This memo is a guide to which translation tricks to use for each pairing.

sections.title: The Available Transition Tools
sections.content:
Three IETF mechanisms are introduced, plus DNS advice:

  • Dual stack (RFC 4213): a dual stack GGSN supports both IPv4 and IPv6 PDP contexts, so dual stack UEs with public addresses can reach both kinds of service without translators. Private IPv4 addresses and NATs are still used in mobile networks.
  • Tunneling: IPv6-in-IPv4 or IPv4-in-IPv6, needing dual stack at both tunnel ends. Tunnels can be static (configured) or dynamic (automatic).
  • Protocol translators: components that let a native IPv4 node and a native IPv6 node talk without changing either, for example NAT-PT (RFC 2766) with SIIT (RFC 2765).

For DNS, the guidance is to keep at least one authoritative server IPv4-enabled and to make sure recursive servers support IPv4, so the name space does not fragment.
sections.eli5: There are three bridges between the old and new address worlds: phones that speak both, tunnels that carry one kind inside the other, and translators that sit in the middle.

sections.title: GPRS Transition Scenarios
sections.content:
Five scenarios from RFC 3574 are analysed. The first two are seen as the most relevant.

  • Dual stack UE: activate an IPv6 PDP context for IPv6 peers and an IPv4 PDP context for IPv4 peers. Operators are strongly urged to deploy basic IPv6 support in their GPRS networks. If the network lacks IPv6 support, the UE may tunnel IPv6 over an IPv4 PDP context.
  • IPv6 UE to an IPv6 node over IPv4: the network handles IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling, so the UE sees native IPv6. The encapsulating node can be the GGSN or an edge router. Manually configured tunnels suit early deployment but become a burden as islands multiply.
  • IPv4 UE to an IPv4 node over IPv6: not considered very likely in 3GPP networks.
  • IPv6 UE to an IPv4 node: IPv6-only UEs are not recommended in early phases. If needed, use specific relays or application proxies, and not generic translation.
  • IPv4 UE to an IPv6 node: legacy UEs are limited to a few applications that already rely on proxies, and the same methods can be used.
sections.eli5: Each pairing of an old or new phone with an old or new website gets its own advice. The best tip is to give phones both languages so they rarely need a translator.

sections.title: IMS Scenarios and UE Configuration
sections.content:
IMS is exclusively IPv6, which cuts the number of scenarios to two: an IPv6 IMS user talking to a node in an IPv4 network, and two IPv6 IMS islands joined across an IPv4 network. The second is closely related to the IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling case and can use similar tunneling.

The first case is harder because SIP signalling and media are separate, and the SDP body in SIP carries the media addresses. The example setup uses an interworking unit made of a dual stack SIP server and a transition gateway (TrGW). The SIP server acts as a B2BUA and rewrites the SDP so the gateway sits in the media path.

This has drawbacks. Rewriting SDP prevents securing the SDP payload end to end, and it breaks end-to-end negotiation of SIP extensions, so new extensions require upgrading the B2BUAs too. The authors call for the SIP-related working groups to specify a better solution quickly.

The RFC also gives an informative overview of how a UE gets its settings: access point configuration, DNS server addresses (via PDP context activation, the PCO-IE, or DHCPv6), and the P-CSCF address.
sections.eli5: Internet phone calls through the phone network only work with the new addresses. To call an old-style phone, a middleman has to rewrite the call details, and that makes the call harder to keep private.

sections.title: Recommendations Summary
sections.content:
The authors' main recommendations are:

  • Dual stack UEs are recommended over IPv4-only or IPv6-only UEs, and applications should be IP version independent.
  • Activate an IPv6 PDP context for IPv6 peers and an IPv4 PDP context for IPv4 peers.
  • Prefer IPv6 over IPv4 going through IPv4 NATs to the same dual stack peer.
  • 3GPP operators should deploy basic IPv6 support in GPRS networks as soon as possible.
  • A lightweight automatic tunneling mechanism should be standardised in the IETF for UEs.
  • A detailed SIP/SDP/media transition solution should be specified as soon as possible.
sections.eli5: The main advice: make phones that speak both languages, switch the network on early, and avoid clumsy translators.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says generic IPv6 deployment security issues are out of its scope. The few techniques it recommends each have their own considerations: tunneling or native upstream access, routing protocols for redundancy, locally deployed relays and application proxies, and a specific mechanism for SIP signalling and media translation.

It does not recommend NAT-PT or another translator as a general-purpose transition mechanism, because of security issues it does not analyse further. An appendix lists 3GPP-specific arguments against generic translators, including that a single translator at the network edge is unlikely to scale to the connections a GGSN handles.
sections.eli5: The memo avoids one risky shortcut, a do-everything translator in the middle, and prefers narrower tools that are easier to keep safe.

items.title: Dual stack
items.text: Node or GGSN speaks both IPv4 and IPv6.

items.title: Tunneling
items.text: IPv6-in-IPv4 or IPv4-in-IPv6, static or dynamic.

items.title: Protocol translators
items.text: A middle component converts between IPv4 and IPv6 without changing the end nodes.
